title: hybrid-transport-slicing-latency-variance-lab-notes-feb-2026
body:
Purpose:
Quick lab notes on the “transport slicing” experiments we ran to understand how mixing HTTP/1.1 long-poll, HTTP/2 multiplexing, and gRPC streaming in the same proxy pool affects latency variance and backpressure amplification. Goal was to surface systemic sources of tail spikes we started seeing in canaries when clients used mixed client libraries (old http1 SDKs + new grpc-http2 SDKs).

High-level hypothesis:
- Multiplexed HTTP/2 streams can hide head-of-line effects, but when combined with proxy egress queueing and large-chunk producers they can cause per-connection bursts that amplify P95/P99 on other streams.
- Client-side pushback (delayed window updates, small write bursts) interacts badly with proxy connection reuse heuristics and causes microbursts and flush clustering.
- We suspect some of the worst tail cases are caused by "egress shadowing": large streaming responses that occupy TCP buffers and trigger probe-based pacing in proxies, delaying unrelated short requests that share the same connection.

Testbed summary:
- Harness: rt-bench-transport-slice v0.3 (Go). Small harness we wrote to drive controlled waveforms across different transports.
- Topology: client -> envoy-ingress (proxy) -> obs-proxy (edge) -> inference-runtime pool (4 nodes, each 8xA100-ish simulated)
- NICs: 25Gbps; machines in the same AZ to avoid cross-region variance.
- Client patterns: mix of 80% short RPCs (prompt-only, 40–120 tokens) and 20% long streamers (prompt+streamed completion, 600–2k tokens).
- Transports tested: HTTP/1.1 chunked (client flush every N tokens), HTTP/2 (multiplexed streams, varying MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS), gRPC (bi-di streaming vs. unary+streaming responses).
- Proxy settings: connection pooling enabled, per-conn egress queue=256 packets, adaptive pacing on; tests toggle pacing on/off.

Key experiments and knobs:
1) Slice traffic by transport (dedicated connection pools per transport) vs mixed pool (single pool for all transports).
2) Vary client write flush frequency: frequent small writes (every 32 tokens) vs large writes (every 512 tokens).
3) Introduce synthetic CPU jitter on backend to mimic kv-cache misses and see amplification.
4) Toggle envoy/ingress adaptive pacing and per-conn queue limits.

Representative metrics (aggregated across 30m runs):
- Mixed pool, pacing ON, small writes:
  - short RPC P50: 9ms, P95: 48ms, P99: 210ms
  - long stream P50 per-chunk: 15ms, P95: 120ms, P99: 680ms
- Dedicated pools per-transport, pacing OFF, small writes:
  - short RPC P50: 8ms, P95: 22ms, P99: 85ms
- Mixed pool, pacing ON, large writes:
  - short RPC P50: 10ms, P95: 55ms, P99: 320ms
- Mixed pool, pacing OFF, small writes:
  - short RPC P50: 11ms, P95: 60ms, P99: 420ms
Notes: Numbers above are coarse but consistent: mixed pool + pacing ON with small writes gave the best P95 for long streams but incurred worst tails for short RPCs. Turning pacing off reduces P95 for short RPCs in some cases but increases tails in others, indicating interplay is non-linear.

Observations / interpretive notes:
- Egress shadowing: when a large streamed response was in-flight on a connection, unrelated short RPCs that got assigned to the same connection saw amplified tails (P99 up 3–5x). This was especially apparent when the client used small frequent writes — the proxy's pacing logic grouped flushes and delayed ACK-window updates.
- Multiplex drift: with HTTP/2, streams with long-lifetime (open bidi streams) were disproportionately responsible for queueing in the proxy. Increasing MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS somewhat mitigated the problem but introduced headroom scheduling overhead.
- Connection reuse heuristics: Envoy's default reuse policy tends to favor reusing connections for new short RPCs; this is good for TLS/session reuse but bad when a connection is occupied by a heavy streamer. Separating pools by transport prevented the allocator from assigning short RPCs to heavy connections and dramatically reduced short-RPC tails.
- Client library behavior matters: older http1 SDKs with synchronous flush semantics created larger bursts at socket level, while upgraded grpc-http2 libs used pacing-friendly coalescing. Mixed client fleets therefore produced asymmetric load that stressed proxies.

Informal failure modes we saw:
- Proxy egress queue full -> backpressure signaled upstream -> client write stalls -> client retransmits or times out (manifested as spike in retry counts).
- Adaptive pacing thrashing: pacing reduced immediate tail but increased variance over longer windows as pacing logic oscillated when traffic waveform changed suddenly.

Quick wins / mitigations to try in prod canary:
- Partition connection pools: use separate pool per transport (http1, http2, grpc) or, at minimum, separate pool for long-lived streamers. Implement quick config in ingress to identify long TTL paths and route to separate upstream cluster.
- Conservative connection assignment: avoid assigning short RPCs to connections with "hot" stream counts or with active large responses. A lightweight per-conn metric (active-streams, bytes-in-flight) in the pool allocator would help.
- Client SDK opt-in: add guidance and an opt-in flag for small-write-friendly coalescing (batch small writes into fewer socket writes) and limit maximum write chunk size for streamers.
- Monitoring: add per-connection queue length telemetry at proxy egress and alert when a single connection is responsible for >20% of queued bytes.

Open questions / next experiments:
- Can we reproduce the same P99 amplification with pure TCP-level load (without proxy)? i.e., is the proxy logic necessary for the effect or would bare connection reuse produce similar shadows?
- Can we tune envoy adaptive pacing parameters to remove oscillation while preserving protection against large bursts? Need to run sweep over pacing alpha/beta values.
- How does QUIC/HTTP3 compare? Hypothesis: QUIC streams per-packet scheduling and handshake differences may reduce shadowing but may introduce different resource sharing patterns on datagrams. Worth a small PoC.

Implementation notes / TODOs:
- PR to rt-bench to add "connection tagging" so we can cause harness to prefer reuse vs new-conn in a controlled percentage. (PR in linked_artifacts).
- Add a lightweight envoy plugin to expose per-conn bytes-in-flight metric to statsd. (Ticket INF-5128).
- Run a 24h soak with production-like mix but with pool partitioning enabled in a canary subset (5% traffic) to measure real-world impact.

Snippets / shorthand:
- run: ./rt-bench -mode=mix -short=80 -long=20 -flush=32 -pool=mixed -pacing=on -dur=30m
- Note to self: compare with basic tcp replay (socat -> open-conn rotate) to isolate proxy vs kernel artifacts.

Slack/refs: #eng-serving-runtime thread "transport-slicing" (link in Confluence). See also: benchmarking notes from Marco (linked_artifacts).

Conclusion (working):
We have a plausible root cause vector: mixed transport fleets + connection reuse + proxy pacing = shadowing that amplifies P99 for short RPCs. Short-term mitigations (pool partitioning + conservative allocator) are low-risk and should be validated in a canary. Longer-term: consider transport-aware scheduling features in the ingress and evaluate QUIC as a potential alternative.

Unresolved: exact pacing parameters that avoid oscillation; impact of client OS TCP stack (coalescing) vs lib-level flush semantics.
